title: Multi-Constraint Logic Puzzles
tagline: Year 4 — Eight-person orderings and five-person, three-attribute grids with many clues and negatives

introduction.overview: Multi-constraint puzzles give more clues than a quick glance can use, so you must process them in order of strength: exact positions first, chains next, either-or splits after that, and negative clues last. Two forms are common: a long ordering with 8 people and a grid with 5 people and 3 attributes. The method is the same: record every clue, merge linked clues into bundles, and test cases only when a clue offers two options.
introduction.placementRelevance: These puzzles carry 4–6 questions and are the usual "difficult set" in the reasoning section.
introduction.realWorldContext: Scheduling and matching with many rules uses the same constraint reasoning.

learningObjectives: Use case splitting for either-or clues
Verify the final arrangement against every clue

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A clue with one possible placement is strongest. Linked clues merge columns. Negative clues only eliminate.

coreDefinitions: Chain: neighbours linked in a fixed order.
Bundle: values known to belong to the same person.
Either-or clue: offers two placements; split into cases.
Verification: checking the result against all clues.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Each clue removes possibilities. Strong clues first means fewer cases later.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: List clues by strength, place the strongest, extend chains, split only when needed, and verify.

mainNarrative: Eight friends in a row: B and A are at the two ends; E is immediately right of B; G is immediately left of D; one person is between E and D; F is immediately right of D; H immediately right of F; C immediately left of A. If A were at the left end, C would need the seat to A's left, which does not exist, so B is at the left end and A at the right end. B, E, then G, D, F, H and C, A.

For the five-person grid, merge links: pilot ↔ Cochin ↔ golf; nurse ↔ Bhopal ↔ squash; hockey ↔ Erode (Chetan); Agra ↔ tennis ↔ chef. Eknath is a clerk who plays kabaddi, so he lives in Dehradun. Disha is the nurse, so she lives in Bhopal and plays squash. Chetan, in Erode, is the tailor who plays hockey. The remaining two, Anil and Bharti, take the pilot and chef bundles; Bharti does not play golf, so Bharti is the chef in Agra playing tennis and Anil is the pilot in Cochin playing golf.
Notice how many clues were redundant for the first deduction: pick the strongest and let the rest confirm.
Negative clues rarely place a person on their own; use them to choose between two remaining options.
Always re-read each clue against the final grid.

deepDiveAspects.title: Redundant clues
deepDiveAspects.content: Some clues confirm what you already know; do not waste time on them until the end.

deepDiveAspects.title: Two-option stalemate
deepDiveAspects.content: If you reach two options with no clue to separate them, a clue was missed or misread.

problemVariations.exampleSnippet: A and B at the ends

solvedExamples.title: Ends clue
solvedExamples.question: B and A sit at the two ends; E is immediately right of B and C is immediately left of A. Who is at the left end?

steps.title: Case A at left
steps.explanation: C would need to be left of A: impossible.

steps.title: So
steps.explanation: B at left, A at right.

solvedExamples.title: Bundle
solvedExamples.question: The pilot lives in Cochin and the golfer is a pilot. Which city does the golfer live in?

solvedExamples.title: Negative clue
solvedExamples.question: Two people (Anil, Bharti) share the pilot and chef bundles and Bharti does not play golf (pilot bundle). Who is the pilot?

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Sort clues by strength, place chains, split either-or clues, apply negatives last and verify.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: An option that breaks any single clue is wrong.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Draw the final grid before answering.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Eight clues do not mean eight steps.

easy.question:
Eight friends A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit in a row facing north. The following facts are known:
1. B and A sit at the two extreme ends (in either order).
2. E sits immediately to the right of B.
3. G sits immediately to the left of D.
4. Exactly 1 person sits between E and D.
5. F sits immediately to the right of D.
6. H sits immediately to the right of F.
7. C sits immediately to the left of A.

Who sits at the left end?
easy.explanation: From left to right the order is B, E, G, D, F, H, C, A; B is at the left end.

advanced.question:
Five friends Anil, Bharti, Chetan, Disha and Eknath each have a different profession (pilot, chef, tailor, nurse, clerk), live in a different city (Agra, Bhopal, Cochin, Dehradun, Erode) and play a different sport (golf, hockey, tennis, kabaddi, squash). The following facts are known:
1. The pilot lives in Cochin.
2. Chetan lives in Erode.
3. The nurse lives in Bhopal.
4. The person who plays golf is a pilot.
5. Eknath is a clerk.
6. The person who lives in Agra plays tennis.
7. The person who plays hockey lives in Erode.
8. The person who plays squash lives in Bhopal.
9. Eknath plays kabaddi.
10. The chef plays tennis.
11. Disha is a nurse.
12. Bharti does not play golf.

What is Anil's profession?
advanced.explanation: Working out the grid gives: Anil: pilot / Cochin / golf; Bharti: chef / Agra / tennis; Chetan: tailor / Erode / hockey; Disha: nurse / Bhopal / squash; Eknath: clerk / Dehradun / kabaddi. So the answer is pilot.
